results.snippet: The present chapter examines Walter ... inspired by Paul Klee’s “Angelus Novus,” presents history as an accumulation of wreckage rather than a path of human improvement....
extra_snippets: The present chapter examines Walter Benjamin’s critique of the ideology of progress as articulated in “On the Concept of History.” Contrasting the conventional linear trajectory of historical advancement, Benjamin, inspired by Paul Klee’s “Angelus Novus,” presents history as an accumulation of wreckage rather than a path of human improvement.

His “angel of history” metaphorically faces the past, propelled forward by the storm of progress into an uncertain future. Benjamin’s work challenges the deterministic views of historical materialism that align progress with the development of productive forces.

He contrasts historicism’s narrative continuity with historical materialism’s obligation to redeem the past, making its obscured moments relevant to the present. The chapter argues that Benjamin’s rejection of teleological and deterministic histories call for a revolutionary historiography that recognizes continuous potential for change and highlights the significance of agency. Additionally, Benjamin’s critique extends to social democracy’s deterministic Marxism, advocating for a praxis-centered, non-linear understanding of historical development.

results.title: Yi Wu, The Historical and Its Discontents: Nietzsche and Benjamin against “Historicism”
results.snippet: This essay seeks to trace from Nietzsche to Benjamin an unbroken yet growing line of critique—of historicism as the “sickness of time” from which modernity suffers, and from which it has been trying to recover. Two attempts at such a recovery will be examined and juxtaposed: The Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life and Theses on the Philosophy of History.
extra_snippets: Representations of historicism as the loss of meaning in history and critiques of historicism as the critique of such a loss had been pervasive since late nineteenth century till the Second World War. Among historicism’s most powerful and representative critics were the young Nietzsche and Benjamin in his Parisian exile.

This essay seeks to trace from Nietzsche to Benjamin an unbroken yet growing line of critique—of historicism as the “sickness of time” from which modernity suffers, and from which it has been trying to recover. Two attempts at such a recovery will be examined and juxtaposed: The Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life and Theses on the Philosophy of History.

By thus situating both historicism and its critiques within the desires and anxieties of modernity, this essay tries to delineate and to understand the peculiarly modernist shapes assumed by the historical and its discontents.

results.snippet: In his famous 1936 essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” Walter Benjamin tells us that in his time art became valued for its exhibition value instead of what he refers to as its secularised ritual or cult value. This essay makes this bold claim plausible by arguing that it means that a historicising gaze no longer has a function in the reception of art.
